title: AI agent security concerns kick-start confidential computing
summary: As incident after incident reveals AI agents running wild and causing security concerns, confidential computing is emerging as a way to lock down AI models in a secure vault. The technology has been slow to catch on, but security concerns around AI and agents — and the need to protect data and models — are sparking renewed interest in it. Traditional encryption protects data in transit and at rest, but not while it’s being used. Confidential computing provides a way to protect data in use. It’s been around for many years, but speed, cost, and complexity have stymied adoption. That may be changing, though, as recent announcements from Intel and Fortanix, which works with Nvidia, make the technology easier to deploy. “The trouble was never belief. It was operational cost, scarce skills, and the awkward truth that protecting the most sensitive workloads can make ordinary troubleshooting harder,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research. AI agents are changing that calculation and fueling confidential computing adoption, Gogia said. How confidential computing works Confidential computing seals AI models and data in a vault, known as a trusted execution environment (TEE), secured by hardware and software. That blocks outside interference, reducing the chances of hackers breaking into systems. The vault unlocks only with a key, which is released after the cryptographic proof that the vault hasn’t been tampered with. The AI model stays inside the vault, where it processes users’ queries and sends back the answers. “AI changed the threat model,” Gogia said, adding, “A model answers. An agent acts.” He continued: “An agent with no access is a verbose intern. An agent with uncontrolled access is an incident report waiting politely in the corridor.” The technology is improving Fortanix is trying to put those agents in the vault. title: Should Apple really move fast and break things?
summary: The Apple ecosystem has more than a billion people in it. Each time the company changes even the tiniest component of that ecosystem, thousands of people complain. Now imagine the reputational damage if Apple began to rush out AI software updates that transformed the user experience so much they actually broke things? Scale matters here: when your active user base is approximately an eighth of the human population, even a pixel of friction generates a backlash. When a butterfly beats its wings… Yet that’s more or less exactly what some Apple analysts seem to think the company should be doing if it wants to keep pace with AI development. They say they think the way Apple is structured — its deliberate, consensus-driven engineering culture and focus on end-to-end integration — is a liability. As they see it, it slows software evolution. They argue that’s why Apple missed the original launch window for Siri AI. Apple’s critics may not be pushing for it to adopt the total chaos of reckless software patches, but their arguments still pretty much mean treating every computer user, government, and business like some vast, unpaid beta-testing pool. Within that worldview, perhaps it doesn’t matter what a billion people using Apple products experience, so long as its operating systems keep pace with whatever hype-powered AI buzzword is being discussed in Silicon Valley. Errors have consequences There is a huge difference between some soon-to-be commodified AI chatbot hallucinating fake information in your browser window and a hallucination taking place inside an operating system actively in your life . “I asked Siri to check my home camera footage, and instead it locked down my whole home, bolted the shutters, and trapped me indoors for a week because the AI hallucinated I was a home invader” may be an exaggeration that reminds you of the hit 1977 movie Demon Seed , but highlights what could happen when probabilistic software meets physical hardware. title: What can a carbon nanotube chip compute for AI?
summary: A carbon nanotube can carry an electrical signal across a transistor. In a chip built at Peking University, thousands of these transistors worked together to recognise handwritten digits. Following one image through the experiment shows which calculations ran on the nanotubes, which ran on a companion chip and how the researchers estimated the power required. A second experiment, fabricated at SkyWater, used nanotubes to bring memory and logic closer together. It demonstrated a different benefit for AI by increasing the rate at which a small memory could supply data. A comparison of devices from universities, chipmakers and materials suppliers explains what each group actually built, from a programmable processor to a wafer of aligned tubes. The remaining industrial question is whether successive production lots can deliver working processors with a measurable energy advantage on the same inference task.

title: Your unit tests are paying an unnecessary DOM tax
summary: Open the test configuration of almost any front-end project and you’ll find one line that decides more about your CI bill than most of the code around it: environment: 'jsdom' . Unit and component tests for React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, and Solid apps rarely run in a real browser. They run in Node.js, on top of a JavaScript implementation of the browser’s Document Object Model. Your test renders a button, clicks it, and asserts on the text that appears. The document, the click() , and the text all come from a library that pretends to be a browser. For most teams that library is jsdom , the long-standing, standards-minded default. A growing number use happy-dom , which is faster but less faithful. Few teams think about the choice again after the first npm install. They should, because the test DOM is often where a component suite spends a large share of its time, and because the two popular options force a trade that most teams don’t know they’re making. Over the past months I measured this on real projects. Here is what I found, and what I built as a result. Where the time goes A component test does very little work of its own. It creates elements, sets attributes, dispatches events, and reads back state. Every one of those steps is a call into the DOM implementation, and DOM APIs are chatty: a single high-level call can fan out into hundreds of internal ones. To see how chatty, I built an open-source tracer, dom-api-tracer , that records which DOM APIs a test suite calls and how often. One example from those traces: a single getComputedStyle() call in jsdom triggered about 1,000 reads of Node and Element properties inside the library, because resolving styles means matching selectors against the tree. Testing libraries call getComputedStyle() constantly, for instance to decide whether an element is visible. Multiply that by tens of thousands of tests and the DOM is no longer a detail. title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
summary: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not (yet?) available as open weights. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! title: Ladybird's first alpha release
summary: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
summary: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible. title: How AI impacted the release of Postgres 19
summary: In the IT calendar, some things are as regular as clockwork — Microsoft Patch Tuesday , for example, telling IT admins every month what they would be working on for the next few weeks. Apple’s developer conference every June showcasing new features to be added into applications in the coming months. The annual release of PostgreSQL was in that same category — every September, the latest version would bring new updates and better performance. This year has been different. This is the first year where AI-assisted development and testing had an impact on contributions and testing, as models like Fable 5, Opus 5, and GPT-6 were released. In September, just when the release candidates would normally be expected, there was a serious discussion about whether the version 19 release would go ahead at all, or whether some of the biggest contributions would have to be removed. Rather than miss this year, the team behind PostgreSQL development decided to postpone the launch to November. Six key features were reverted , including several major additions that the community wanted, like the big feature for this year SQL/PGQ (property graph query) support and online enabling and disabling of data checksums. It is important to recognize the sheer amount of work that takes place around PostgreSQL versions, and how much goes into each update both for new functionality and for improving performance and reliability. PostgreSQL is one of the biggest community open source projects, and it has led the way in demonstrating how a mix of companies and individuals can come together in order to keep innovating. However, we can’t risk shipping what the community is not happy with or where there are multiple known problems. Getting a consistent response in place One of the biggest changes in PostgreSQL 19 is the introduction of REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) .
